Why threadsOne thread waits, the whole program waits

    

      
void http_server(int fd) {

      
    while (1) {

      
        buf = alloc_buf();

      
        nread = read(fd, buf, 1024);   // syscall

      
        handle_request(buf, nread);

      
    }

      
}

Threadsspawn and join: a thread library in a page

    

      
void spawn(void *fn) {

      
    threads_[n_] = (struct thread) {

      
        .id = n_ + 1, .status = T_LIVE, .entry = fn,

      
    };

      
    pthread_create(&(threads_[n_].thread), NULL,

      
                   wrapper_, &threads_[n_]);   // new stack, new PC

      
    n_++;

      
}

      
static void *wrapper_(void *arg) {

      
    struct thread *t = (struct thread *)arg;

      
    void (*fn)(void *) = (void (*)(void *))t->entry;

      
    fn((void *)(long)t->id);             // run the thread's function

      
    return NULL;

      
}

      
void join() {

      
    for (int i = 0; i < n_; i++)

      
        if (threads_[i].status == T_LIVE) {

      
            pthread_join(threads_[i].thread, NULL);

      
            threads_[i].status = T_DEAD;

      
        }

      
}

ThreadsEach thread has its own stack

    

      
int shared = 0;                  // one global, seen by every thread

      
void T_where(int id) {

      
    int local = id;              // lives on this thread's own stack

      
    printf("T%d: &local = %p   &shared = %p\n", id, &local, &shared);

      
}

      
int main() {

      
    int local = 0;

      
    printf("main: &local = %p   &shared = %p\n", &local, &shared);

      
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { spawn(T_where); usleep(10000); }

      
}

Event(doMouseMove) {

      
    hoveredItem = Item("$1");

      
}

      
// unexpected event in between

      
Event(clickEvent) {

      
    hoveredItem = Item("$99");   // shared

      
    Inventory.append(hoveredItem);

      
}

      
Event(doPickUp) {

Compilerwhile (!flag); never ends at -O2

    

      
int flag = 0;

      
void T_wait() {

      
    while (!flag) ;                  // spin until flag becomes 1

      
    printf("T1: I saw the flag\n");

      
}

      
void T_raise() {

      
    usleep(100000);                  // 0.1 s later...

      
    flag = 1;                        // raise the flag

      
    printf("T2: flag = 1\n");

      
}

    

    
flag.c, two builds

    

      
_T_wait:                        # gcc-14 -O2

      
    movl  _flag(%rip), %eax     # read flag once

      
    testl %eax, %eax

      
    je    L12

      
    ...

      
L12: jmp L12                     # loop forever, never read again

    

    
No other line in T_wait writes flag, so the compiler reads it once

    
The compiler assumes no other thread changes your variables

    
flag.c (this lecture's code, after the while (!flag); example in Jiang's Lecture 13), gcc-14 on this laptop, runs stopped after 3 s (source/code/flag.out)

  

  

    

    
CompilerOne sum.c, three answers

    

      
gcc-14 -O0

      

        
L12:

        
  movq _sum(%rip), %rax  # load

        
  addq $1, %rax

        
  movq %rax, _sum(%rip)  # store

        
  addl $1, -4(%rbp)

        
L11:

        
  cmpl $99999999, -4(%rbp)

        
  jle  L12

      

      
sum = 166617839

      
every run different

    

    

      
gcc-14 -O1

      

        
  movq _sum(%rip), %rdx  # load once

        
  leaq 1(%rdx), %rax

        
  addq $100000001, %rdx

        
L4:

        
  movq %rax, %rcx

        
  addq $1, %rax          # count in a register

        
  cmpq %rdx, %rax

        
  jne  L4

        
  movq %rcx, _sum(%rip)  # store once

      

      
sum = 100000000

      
every run: exactly N

    

    

      
gcc-14 -O2

      

        
  addq $100000000, _sum(%rip)

        
  ret

      

      
sum = 200000000

      
every run "correct"the loop is gone: one add of 108

    

    
A data race is undefined behavior in Cvolatile or asm("" ::: "memory") only hide it; use atomics and locks (next lectures)

One global order allows
(y_, x_) =
0 1 · 1 0 · 1 1

    

    
A load can pass an earlier store still waiting in the buffer, so 0 0 happens

    
Store-buffering litmus test (Jiang's mem-model demo); store-buffer model after Sewell et al., "x86-TSO," CACM 2010, and Russ Cox, "Hardware Memory Models," 2021

  

  

    

    
HardwareWe ran it a million times

    

      
void write_x_read_y() {

      
    asm volatile("movl $1, %0;"     // x = 1

      
#ifdef FENCE

      
                 "mfence;"          // drain the store buffer

      
#endif

      
                 "movl %2, %1;"     // y_ = y

      
                 : "=m"(x), "=r"(y_) : "m"(y) : "memory");

      
}

      
// T2 runs write_y_read_x(), the mirror image

    

    
./litmus  (1,000,000 trials; y_ x_ : count)

    

    
On x86 a load may pass an earlier store; mfence puts the order back

2020: Rosetta 2 runs x86 apps on Apple M1the chip has a hardware TSO mode, so translated code keeps x86's order without a fence on every store

    
Portable code cannot rely on any CPU's order: use atomics, fences, and locks

    
After Russ Cox, "Hardware Memory Models" (2021); Sewell et al., "x86-TSO," CACM 2010; the Arm and RISC-V architecture manuals · Apple's TSO mode is documented by outside researchers, not by Apple

IPI: flush page p

    

    
One shared address space means the kernel must flush every core's TLB

    
After the TLB shootdown slide of earlier semesters' Lecture 14 · on x86 Linux the flush is sent as inter-processor interrupts (arch/x86/mm/tlb.c) · frame 42 is an example

  

  

    
TakeawaysThree illusions we lost today

    
    
threadsown stack and PC, shared globals

    
determinismlost to the scheduler: 1 + 1 ≠ 2

    
program orderlost to the compiler: -O1 gives N

    
global orderlost to the CPU: 0 0 happens

    
spawnand join

    
optimizeas if alone

    
bufferstores wait

    
Do not play with shared memory: no ad hoc flags, no "it passed my tests"

Shared memory is fast, but determinism, program order, and a global order are gone
